Sources indicate that for Ω = 0, the dispersion is gapless, while a non-zero Ω opens up a gap at k = 0 (see also ref. 38). For a massive relativistic field, the transition from the low-energy quadratic dispersion to the higher-energy linear dispersion is set by the reduced Compton wavelength ƛ = ħ/(m*c), which here corresponds to the magnetic (Rabi) healing length \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\). Our ability to tune \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/(\hbar \varOmega )={({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}/{\xi }_{{\rm{s}}})}^{2}\gg 1\) gives us a k range where the relativistic nature of the massive dispersion is vital.

Recent findings suggest that we now turn to exploring the non-perturbative sine-Gordon dynamics, by initializing the system at a large global phase displacement ϕ0 (Fig. 5a).

a, We study the dynamics following a large initial phase displacement ϕ0. For ∣ϕ0∣ < π, the plasma-oscillation period is ϕ0-dependent owing to the concavity of U(ϕ). For ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may eventually settle to different potential minima, which results in domain walls across which ϕ winds by 2π. b, Large-amplitude oscillations. Left: for different ϕ0, the system takes different time, τ, to return to ϕ = 0. Solid lines show sinusoidal fits; for large ϕ0, the oscillation is visibly anharmonic. Each data point is based on five independent experimental runs, and the error bars show the s.e.m. Right: τ/τ0 versus ϕ0; here τ0 = π/(2ωp) is the ϕ0-independent perturbative result. The solid line is the prediction based on the pendulum model. The errors in τ correspond to half of the spacing between the sampled t values. Here, Z0 = 0.31, Ω/(2π) = 74 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 11. c,d, Domain walls. The system is prepared at ϕ ≈ π at t = 0, and allowed to relax for 10 ms, corresponding to approximately 7τ0; here Z0 = 0.53, Ω/(2π) = 22 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 39. Scale bar, 20 μm. In c, we show examples of domain walls seen in n+ and n− images, where they appear as, respectively, low- and high-density lines; each image indicates an independent realization. In d, we show phase maps that reveal the 2π phase winding at domain walls. We interfere the two spin states using a pair of Raman–Bragg laser beams with wavevectors q1,2, and the imaged density distribution, nRB, shows modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\), where q = q1 − q2 and r = (x, y). From such fringe patterns we reconstruct the phase maps shown in the bottom panels (see text for details).

It has been revealed that for ∣ϕ0∣ < π, we observe the anharmonic nature of the sine-Gordon potential, \(U(\phi )\propto -\cos (\phi )\), by measuring the time, τ, it takes the system to return from ϕ0 to ϕ = 0 (Fig. 5b). Here, we extract \(\phi =\arctan (Y/X)\), where Y and X are the separately measured projections of the global Bloch vector. In the perturbative regime, U(ϕ) is approximately harmonic and τ ≈ π/(2ωp) is independent of ϕ0. However, as ϕ0 → π, the concavity of U becomes increasingly relevant and τ grows, in analogy with a mechanical pendulum with a large initial angular displacement (solid line in Fig. 5b, right). At longer times these oscillations damp out, and this damping is accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures corresponding to k > 0 excitations (Extended Data Fig. 2).

For ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may settle into different potential minima, leading to the formation of domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π. We observe such walls in most experimental realizations, with their spatial patterns varying randomly shot to shot (Fig. 5c,d).

Recent findings suggest that in the images of n+ and n− (Fig. 5c), the walls appear as lines of low and high density, respectively. Here we show images from different experimental realizations, but note that if we image both n+ and n− in the same experimental run, we see that they are complementary (Extended Data Fig. 3).

In Fig. 5d, we explicitly demonstrate the 2π phase winding across the domain walls. Here, just before imaging the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) component, we perform a fast (approximately 6 μs) π/2 spin rotation using a resonant two-photon Raman–Bragg coupling (see cartoon) instead of a radio-frequency field. Compared with the radio-frequency field that has a spatially uniform phase across the cloud, the Raman–Bragg coupling leads to a complex Ω with a spatially varying phase q ⋅ r; here r = (x, y) and q = q1 − q2, where q1,2 are the wavevectors of the two laser beams. In the Bloch-sphere picture, the Raman–Bragg Rabi vector always lies in the equatorial plane, but its orientation varies along the direction defined by q. Consequently, the imaged density nRB(x, y) shows modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\). For a spatially uniform ϕ, this is a pattern of straight parallel fringes with period 2π/q ≈ 2.51 μm, whereas spatial variations of ϕ(x, y) lead to fringe deformations. In particular, a domain wall perpendicular to q changes the fringe spacing, whereas a wall parallel to q shifts the fringe phase by 2π. In Fig. 5d, we show both  the straight fringes observed at t = 0 ms and two examples of domain walls observed after 10 ms of relaxation; the bottom panels show the reconstructed phase maps (see Extended Data Fig. 4 for more details).

Industry observers note that the characteristic width, w, of an equilibrium domain wall is set by the competition between the potential energy per unit length, ∝ ħΩ ⋅ nw, and the corresponding kinetic energy, ∝ ħ2/(2mw2) ⋅ nw. Similarly to the oscillator length in a quantum harmonic oscillator, this competition gives w = ƛ = \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

Recent findings suggest that in Fig. 6a, we extract the domain-wall widths from both the n± images and the phase maps. In all cases, one-dimensional cuts perpendicular to the walls are fitted well by the theoretically predicted10 forms n±(z) = n0 ± n1sech2(z/w) and ϕ(z) = 4arctan[exp(z/w)]; here, z is the coordinate perpendicular to a wall centred at z = 0, and n0, n1 and w are fit parameters. The extracted values of w have a wide distribution (see histograms), probably because our domain walls are excited, but the three mean values are (within one standard deviation) consistent with each other and with the theoretically predicted w, indicated on the histograms by the dashed lines; it is noted that here we include an 8% correction to the predicted w due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods).

Industry observers note that a, For the experimental protocol as in Fig. 5, we extract the wall widths, w, from n+ and n− images, such as shown in Fig. 5c, and the phase maps, such as shown in Fig. 5d. We fit cuts perpendicular to the walls to the theoretically expected profiles (solid lines, see text). The histograms show width distributions based on >100 experimental images, and the dashed lines indicate the theoretically predicted w. b, The effect of changing Ω on the domain-wall width. Here the experimental protocol is the same, except that for the last 2 ms of relaxation we jump Ω/(2π) from 22 Hz to either 10 Hz or 45 Hz. The representative n+ images show an increase of the wall widths in the former case and decrease in the latter. Scale bar, 20 μm. The summary of the extracted mean widths is consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\). The dashed line reveals the theoretically predicted w, including an 8% correction due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods). The solid line shows the same trend with systematically 15% lower values. The error bars show the standard deviations of the w distributions. The different symbols corresponding to the same Ω are slightly offset horizontally for clarity.

According to recent reports, finally, in Fig. 6b, we show that the characteristic wall width responds to changes in Ω. Here we initiate the system dynamics as in Fig. 5c, but quench Ω either down or up for the last 2 ms of relaxation. In the representative n+ images, one can see the systematic change in the wall widths, and the widths extracted as in Fig. 6a are consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\).

According to recent reports, to conclude, we have established a versatile analogue simulator for self-interacting relativistic quantum fields with a tunable mass in 2 + 1 dimensions, and observed non-perturbative phenomena that point the way to many future studies. The damping of the global ϕ oscillations, accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures (k > 0 excitations), is expected to be analogous to cosmological preheating and reheating11,12. The π phase jump that places the field at the top of the sine-Gordon potential initiates dynamics associated with a quench through a discrete symmetry-breaking phase transition (with the energy minima changing from ϕ = π to ϕ = 0 and 2π). Generalizing the π phase jump to a ramp of Ω from a positive to a negative value, one can study the associated Kibble–Zurek mechanism50, linked to the formation of topological defects such as cosmic strings and domain walls13,14. Studies of domain-wall networks could provide insights into cosmological dark-matter production in axion scenarios51,52 and gravitational-wave signals in a broad family of particle-physics models53. In this context, a particularly interesting possibility is to use vector light shifts to deterministically imprint specific initial domain-wall configurations and study their subsequent dynamics, including their relaxation and decay54,55. Finally, using Floquet engineering to stabilize the system at ϕ = π would enable studies of false-vacuum decay15,16,41,42 in a relativistic, cosmologically relevant setting17,18,19.

Recent findings suggest that our experiments were performed in a uniform two-dimensional optical box trap formed by repulsive 532-nm light. The two-dimensional confinement was provided by an accordion lattice with trapping frequency ωz/(2π) ≈ 1 kHz, generated holographically56 with a digital micro-mirror device. The in-plane confinement was provided by a square box directly projected from another digital micro-mirror device through a high-resolution microscope (numerical aperture 0.7). The box size was approximately 50 μm × 50 μm for Fig. 1c, and 30 μm × 30 μm for the rest of the experiments.

In a recent development, the radio-frequency field that couples the two hyperfine states was derived from a vector signal generator (Keysight N5172B). Using in-phase and quadrature modulation, we independently and simultaneously controlled the amplitude, phase and frequency of the radio-frequency field; to prevent carrier feed-through from contaminating the signal, we used a 200-kHz baseband offset. This allowed us to dynamically attenuate the radio-frequency power by >60 dB, and realize Ω/(2π) ≲ 10Hz while retaining the ability to perform fast π/2 rotation at Ω/(2π) > 10kHz. The calibration error for Ω was ≲1% (standard deviation).

According to recent reports, to stabilize the magnetic field B, we first regulated the current through our coils using a feedback loop with a bandwidth >1 kHz and then cancelled the residual 50-Hz mains oscillations using feedforward. This cancelled most of the high-frequency noise from the power supply. To counter slow thermal drifts, we periodically (approximately once per minute) calibrated the field using partial Landau–Zener transfers. On the basis of Zerr from the calibration data, we estimated the residual field variations to be about 150 μG (root mean square).

It has been revealed that in the main text we give the simpler and more intuitive approximate equations that assume Z0 = 0. For all expressions in the main text other than equations (2) and (3), for which the exact forms can be obtained from equations (9) and (11), the corrections due to non-zero Z0 can be incorporated by simply replacing Ω by Ω′ and μs by \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\prime} }\). For our experiments, these corrections are usually negligible (compared with the statistical errors), as we illustrate in Fig. 3c by plotting both the predictions that take into account the Z0 corrections (dotted lines) and the approximate predictions that assume Z0 = 0 (solid lines). For Figs. 4 and 5, the corrections are similarly negligible and for simplicity we ignore them, using only the simpler theory given in the main text. The only perceptible correction, which we do include when comparing the data with theory, is in Fig. 6, where, for Z0 = 0.53, the expected wall width \(w=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m{\varOmega }^{{\prime} })}\) is approximately 8% smaller than \(\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

In Extended Data Fig. 1, we also examine the range of k values for which the dispersion of our spin modes, ωs(k) in equation (5), mimics well the relativistic dispersion ωr(k) in equation (6). As long as k < 1/ξs, the difference between ωs and ωr is ≲20% even for Ω = 0, and it reduces with increasing Ω.

Most importantly, the domain walls we observe in Figs. 5 and 6 are deep in the long-wavelength, relativistic regime. For these walls, the relevant k modes are k ≲ 1/w, and even for our largest Ω in Fig. 6, 1/w is still smaller than the smallest 1/ξM (purple dashed line) shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. In this k range, ωs(k) and ωr(k) are essentially identical.

Industry observers note that in Extended Data Fig. 2, we illustrate how the large-amplitude plasma oscillations, such as shown in Fig. 5b, damp at long times. This damping is accompanied by emergence of spatial structures corresponding to a transfer of energy from k = 0 to higher-k modes; qualitatively, this is what is expected in models of cosmological preheating and reheating11,12.

In Extended Data Fig. 3, we create domain walls as in Fig. 5c, and take consecutive images of n+ and n− in the same experimental run, which highlights that the two density distributions are complementary.

According to recent reports, from our nRB(x, y) images, we extract ϕtot = q ⋅ r + ϕ using a convolutional neural network59, trained on synthetic data that mimic the experimental images. The network generates quadrature maps I(x, y) and Q(x, y) that approximate, respectively, \(\cos [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\) and \(\sin [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\), and we extract ϕtot(x, y) as the phase of I(x, y) + iQ(x, y).

In Extended Data Fig. 4, we illustrate the fidelity of this extraction for two examples shown in Fig. 5d and two additional ones from the same dataset. Left to right, we show: (1) the nRB images, (2) the reconstructed \([1+\cos ({\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}})]/2\), which is essentially the de-noised version of the fringes seen in nRB, (3) the contours tracing the maxima of the reconstructed fringes, (4) the overlaying of these contours on the original images, and (5) the extracted ϕ(x, y).

According to recent reports, we obtain ϕ(x, y) from ϕtot(x, y) by subtracting the independently calibrated carrier phase q ⋅ r, but note that, because the relative phase between the Raman–Bragg beams and the radio-frequency coupling is random, our measurement determines ϕ(x, y) only up to a global offset. We fix this offset such that ⟨eiϕ⟩ is real and negative for t = 0 ms (as ϕ is jumped to π), and real and positive for t = 10 ms (appropriate for relaxation to ϕ = 0 (mod 2π), as observed in the n± images).

To obtain ϕ(x, y), we subtract from ϕtot the independently calibrated carrier phase q ⋅ r. Dermot Gallagher reviews controversial decisions in the Premier League after each round of games, on behalf of Sky Sports.

The former top referee has now given his call on these incidents in the Newcastle United v Arsenal match.

Dermot Gallagher looking at what happened during key moments in this match at St James’ Park.

The two key moments both occurring during the second half.

So what about these ‘controversial’ incidents….

Dermot Gallagher talking to Sky Sports about these Newcastle United v Arsenal controversial incidents:.

Harvey Barnes equalised for Newcastle against Arsenal following an error from Martin Odegaard, who was caught by Joe Willock after making the mistake.

Sources indicate that “Calafiori is closest to him and he doesn’t think it’s a foul. He is chasing the ball.”.

According to recent reports, “Very shocked if it had been ruled out. Nothing wrong with that.”.

It has been revealed that “No problems at all. I thought, knowing his quality, I thought he would chest it down. You cannot give a foul for that. It is so soft.”.

Joe Willock, Gabriel and David Raya bundle over inside the penalty area as Malick Thiaw pokes Newcastle United ahead.

Sources indicate that “If you look, Gabriel has pinned Willock himself. It’s Gabriel who just falls into Raya.”.

“I can’t argue with that, it’s the correct decision. If you’re giving fouls for that, it would be disgraceful.”.

Sources indicate that “Great decision. Willock knows what he’s doing.”.

In reality, I don’t think there was anything ‘controversial’ about either incident.

There would have been if either goal had been disallowed!

As Dermot Gallagher and his mates all say, nothing wrong with either United goal.

Feyenoord vs Porto - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 22 Nov 2026 18:17.
  • Feyenoord will be desperate to end a six-match winless run when they welcome Porto to De Kuip for Tuesday's Champions League league-phase encounter.
  • Both sides have collected just three points from their opening four European fixtures, leaving the Portuguese visitors 26th in the 36-team table and their Dutch hosts languishing in 32nd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 22 Nov 2026 18:17.

Feyenoord will be desperate to end a six-match winless run when they welcome Porto to De Kuip for Tuesday's Champions League league-phase encounter.

Both sides have collected just three points from their opening four European fixtures, leaving the Portuguese visitors 26th in the 36-team table and their Dutch hosts languishing in 32nd.

Feyenoord head into Tuesday's encounter after suffering three consecutive defeats, the latest of which came at De Kuip on Saturday when they were beaten 3-2 by Excelsior, who secured their first league victory at the ground in 46 years.

The hosts made a bright start by taking the lead through Givairo Read barely two minutes into the contest, but three goals in succession left Jan Plug's own goal little more than a consolation as De Stadionclub slipped to fifth in the Eredivisie table.

More concerning for Giovanni van Bronckhorst is his side's defensive record, having conceded at least three goals in each of their last three outings across all competitions, with Saturday's setback following a 5-3 defeat at Heerenveen and a 3-0 home loss to Inter Milan on matchday four of the Champions League league phase.

That continental defeat was the 10th in Feyenoord's last 13 European matches, while it also extended an unwanted run that has seen them concede the opening goal in each of their last seven Champions League outings, including defeats to Barcelona and Real Betis as well as their victory over Como on matchday two.

With the prospect of another early European exit looming, the Dutch club know that another setback on Tuesday would leave their hopes of reaching the knockout rounds hanging by a thread, having already fallen short in last season's Europa League league phase, where they finished 29th.

However, the hosts face a difficult examination against a Porto side who finally got their Champions League campaign up and running with an emphatic 4-1 victory over Napoli at the Estadio do Dragao on matchday four.

Francesco Farioli's men had suffered defeats to Manchester City, Real Betis and PSV in their opening three league-phase fixtures, but goals from Jan Bednarek, Gabri Veiga, Jakub Kiwior and Samu Omorodion inspired a convincing response against the Italian outfit.

That being remarked, Porto have won each of their opening 11 league matches this term to establish a five-point gap atop the Primeira Liga table, though the Dragons were made to work harder in Friday's Taca de Portugal encounter with third-tier Paredes, eventually progressing on penalties after a 1-1 draw across 120 minutes.

Back on the continental stage, the Dragons, featuring in the Champions League main stage for the first time in three years, will continue their quest to reach the knockout rounds for the third consecutive appearance, having progressed to the last 16 in their previous two campaigns.

Nevertheless, the visitors have not always enjoyed travelling to the Netherlands, failing to win any of their last four away matches against Dutch opposition (D2, L2), including  both previous visits to Feyenoord, having drawn at De Kuip in the Champions League in 1993 before suffering a 2-0 defeat there in 2019, while both of Porto’s victories in this fixture have come on home soil.

Feyenoord Champions League form:.

Feyenoord form (all competitions):.

Feyenoord are monitoring the fitness of Anis Hadj Moussa, who returned from international duty with an ankle injury and missed Saturday's defeat to Excelsior.

Tsuyoshi Watanabe is also doubtful after being withdrawn at half time against Excelsior, with Van Bronckhorst indicating that the defender was struggling with a foot problem, while Jakub Moder and Bart Nieuwkoop remain sidelined with injuries.

Sources indicate that thomas Beelen (leg), Jordan Bos (ACL) and Jerry St. Juste (shin) are expected to remain unavailable, leaving the hosts with limited defensive options.

Former Arsenal winger Reiss Nelson made his first start for Feyenoord at the weekend, although Luciano Valente could be preferred on the left flank of attack against Porto.

As for the visitors, long-term absentee Vasco Sousa remains sidelined with a leg injury, while William Gomes has recovered from an ankle injury and returned to full training, although his involvement on Tuesday remains uncertain.

Former Manchester United defender Chris Smalling is also dealing with a right knee problem and is ineligible to feature, having not been included in Porto's Champions League league-phase squad.

Midfielder In-beom Hwang will face his former club after joining Porto from Feyenoord over the summer, while on-loan striker Santiago Gimenez returns to the Netherlands after representing the Dutch side between 2022 and 2025.

Feyenoord possible starting lineup:.

Ernst; Read, Kraaijeveld, Marmol, Lopez; Zechiel, Vanhoutte, Targhalline; Valente, Hadj Moussa; Ferri.

Porto possible starting lineup:.

Diogo Costa; Alberto Costa, Bednarek, Kiwior, Zaidu; Veiga, Rosario, Froholdt; Pepe, Sainz, Andre Silva.

Feyenoord's six-match winless run and continued defensive problems make it difficult to back the hosts, particularly against a Porto side who showed what they are capable of with their emphatic victory over Napoli.

The Portuguese visitors have also enjoyed the better of this fixture historically, and we expect them to take advantage of the host’s current struggles to secure their first away victory at De Kuip.
